Chapter 3: Making Peace with Food and Removing Guilt.
Now that you’ve started letting go of strict diet rules and are learning to listen to your body, let’s talk about something truly liberating—making peace with food itself.
Imagine what it would feel like to drop the idea that some foods are “good” and others are “bad.” Instead, what if you could approach every bite with a sense of curiosity, maybe even a little excitement, but without the baggage of judgment?
For so many of us, food has carried a ton of moral meaning. Think about it—a slice of cake might be labeled a “guilty pleasure,” while a salad feels “virtuous.” These kinds of labels don’t just change how we see food... they actually create cycles of deprivation and rebellion.
You might’ve noticed that when certain foods are off-limits, they start to feel almost irresistible. And if you do eat them, guilt or shame can come rushing in.
So, what does it really mean to make peace with food?
It’s about giving yourself unconditional permission to eat anything. Yep, you heard that right—all foods.
Now, this doesn’t mean eating without caring how you feel. It’s about removing the emotional charge that comes from making foods forbidden. When nothing’s off-limits, the urge to overeat just isn’t as strong anymore.
Here’s a way to picture it: imagine telling a child they can never have a certain toy. That toy suddenly becomes the only thing they want, right? But if the toy’s always available, the magic fades, and the child can decide if they want to play with it—no drama.
So, how can you put this into practice?
Start by noticing which foods you’ve labeled as “bad” or off-limits.
How do you feel just thinking about eating them?
Then, try bringing one of those foods into your life in a calm, mindful way. Maybe you pick up a favorite snack, sit down without distractions, and really notice the taste, the texture, and how satisfying it feels.
Pay attention to how your body responds. Does this food bring you comfort? Pleasure? Or maybe a bit of discomfort?
Is the urge to overeat as strong as you expected, or is it actually a little less intense?
You can repeat this with other foods—gradually building trust that, honestly, nothing is banned anymore.
Over time, those once-forbidden foods lose their grip. Someone who felt totally out of control around chocolate might realize it’s just another option—something to enjoy or skip, based on what they really want.
There’s another piece to this puzzle: letting go of guilt.
Guilt is heavy, and it usually leads to more eating, not less.
If you can approach your food choices with real curiosity, not judgment, you open up space to learn.
Maybe a certain meal leaves you feeling sluggish. That’s just information—not a reason to beat yourself up.
Real stories bring this to life. Picture someone who used to binge on chips in secret, weighed down by shame. When they start eating chips openly and mindfully, something amazing happens—the power those chips once held just fades. Sometimes a handful is enough, and sometimes, they realize, they actually want something else entirely.
Making peace with food isn’t a quick fix—it’s a journey of healing.
It’s about swapping fear and guilt for trust and enjoyment, and realizing that every food can have a place in a balanced, satisfying life.
